title: Local birders count for global event
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Local birders count for global event

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 793
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County birders brought out both binoculars and spotting scopes to help them identify grackles, eagles and wood ducks near Kingston Landing Launch on the Choptank on Sunday.They identify different species using many criteria, like song, flight pattern and distinctive markings.
Some birders even brought long-lensed cameras to back up their identifications with photographic evidence.
The international Great Backyard Bird Count took place from Feb. 16 to 19. Birders from all over the world went out to see what was flying and then sent the data via eBird, the world's largest database of birds, back to Cornell University.
Birders identify different species using many criteria, like song, flight pattern and distinctive markings.
The birds rarely sit still to be counted, but bird counting efforts can help indicate species health and range, birders said.
Birding discoveries can reflect climate change and loss of habitat. For example, for the first time ever, it is warm enough to find glossy ibis in Maryland. This bird is more commonly found in Florida.
"Good data goes to eBird. It is an international database that is free for the use of the scientific community. What we are doing as citizens goes to enrich the scientific information. eBird started roughly 20 years ago. This weekend is a citizen science weekend. There are maybe 50 people from Talbot County participating. Some on walks like this — we had 24 at Pickering Creek on Friday. And some just in their backyard," said Wayne Bell, PhD, as he ventured out with the group Sunday.
Bell, who teaches a class on Birds and Birding on the Eastern Shore at the Chesapeake Forum, likes birding because it gets him outside with a bunch of nice people.
What looks like a brown lump in deep camouflage is an identifiable species to him. There is a skilled eye and ear to develop in birding.
What birders discover varies greatly based on location and season, he said.
"We are right in the shoulder. The waterfowl are leaving and the spring migration hasn't quite started yet. We are looking at the dead of winter," Bell said.
By coming together globally, birding groups help gather useful local data that is aggregated by eBird into a global picture.
"There is a paper that came out in 2019 that got a lot of traction that documents the decline in North American bird populations by a third. We have lost 30% of our birds in the last 50 years. Loss of habitat. They didn't go anywhere, they are gone," Bell said. "The global warming thing is kicking in in the last 50 years. Most of it is loss of habitat. One exception to that has been waterbirds."
The person leading the frigid morning count Feb. 18 was Bettye Maki, president of the Talbot Bird Club.
"The Great Backyard Bird Count lasts for four days. For all the four days, you could do it everyday. I have gotten feedback from the eBird people. They have people who monitor, and if they don't agree or they think you are wrong about something, they let you know. They are very helpful. They give me more information," Maki said.
She has traveled all over the world to see birds and has 700 species identified. She saw around 30 to 40 on this bird count.
Maki said she likes to encourage new birders. She will give a talk at the Chesapeake Forum in the spring about her trip to Borneo.
"You have to like to be outdoors. There is the camaraderie and the ability to learn while seeing and doing this. There is the diversity of what you are seeing. It is like an Easter egg hunt. It is just fun," Maki said. "It is like fishing — some days are good and some days it isn't. But you always have a wonderful day outdoors. I always feel better for doing it."
Talbot County Bird Club has 80 members.
Another member of the Bird Club is Dave Burgevin. Not only was he geared up with a 500mm lens and binoculars, but he could convincingly call out to the birds in their songs, chirps and shrieks.
"I started learning the calls when I was 10 with Cornell birders. So it was like learning an instrument early. My dad got me into birding before I was six. I learned to tell the difference in the calls. I have continued to lead bird walks over the past 30 years in Maryland and Northern Virginia," said Burgevin.
He said the bird count is important.
"It is a worldwide effort to learn about migration and species decline or increase," he said
He has numbers backing up his passion.
"There are about 400 species available in Maryland including migration. There is about 888 available in the US. The country with the most is Columbia at about 1,800. There are just under 10,000 worldwide," said Burgevin.

title: Ghrist sponsors DAF storage bill
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Ghrist sponsors DAF storage bill

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — State Del. Jeff Ghrist introduced legislation Feb. 9 aimed at giving local jurisdictions the authority to regulate the storage of dissolved air flotation by-products, otherwise known as DAF residuals."I want to make sure that the local governing bodies can do that on their own without any ambiguity, because small counties like Caroline … can't afford to be sued," Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) said in a Feb. 21 interview.
House Bill 1404 was co-sponsored by Del. Steve Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) and Del. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) as well as two Cecil County legislators and three from the western shore. It is cross-filed with Senate Bill 1149, sponsored by Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico).
Ghrist's bill addresses an issue the Caroline County Commissioners have been dealing with in their legislation process since mid-December. He said he discussed the DAF storage issue with the commissioners, the Eastern Shore delegation and the Maryland Farm Bureau.
Neither the state's Department of the Environment nor the Department of Agriculture have jurisdiction over regulating or controlling the storage of DAF residuals, "and so we have at least one person taking advantage of that loophole in the law," he said.
"Whether or not (Love's bill) removes any ambiguity (regarding) how much control the county commissioners have in storage, that remains to be seen," Ghrist said. "But I just want to make sure that after this legislation is passed that one, it goes far enough to ensure that we're not going to have DAF being stored anywhere near our towns, and two, if it doesn't go far enough, I want to make sure that the local governing bodies can (restrict it) on their own, without any ambiguity."
Ghrist said he wanted to make sure that the case would have no standing in court if "anybody decided to sue the county."
The bill is "just a placeholder," Ghrist said. If a separate bill, HB991 sponsored by Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery) addresses the DAF storage issue and is passed, Ghrist said he may consider withdrawing his.
If enacted, HB991 would establish an industrial sludge utilization permit administered and enforced by the Department of the Environment.
Ghrist's bill will be considered 1 p.m. March 8 by the Environment and Transportation Committee.
Love's bill will go to the same committee 1 p.m. March 5.
For more information on legislation in the 2024 Maryland General Assembly, visit mgaleg.maryland.gov.

title: Maryland lawmakers urge Congress to spend more on Chesapeake Bay restoration
author: YESENIA MONTENEGRO and BRENNAN STEWART Capital News Service
content:
Maryland lawmakers urge Congress to spend more on Chesapeake Bay restoration

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: YESENIA MONTENEGRO and BRENNAN STEWART Capital News Service | Section: National 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — Citing encouraging signs of improvement, five Maryland lawmakers expressed their support Wednesday for increased funding of the federally-backed Chesapeake Bay restoration program."We've made progress," Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.) said at a luncheon hosted by the Choose Clean Water Coalition. "We have the least amount of dead zones that we've seen since the 1980s on the bay. We have underwater grasses that are coming back in the Chesapeake Bay. We have oyster crops that we never thought we'd be able to see starting to bloom in the Chesapeake Bay. We're not at our historic levels, not even close. I understand that. But we've made progress."
The coalition, which was started in 2009, hosted its 13th annual Chesapeake Bay Day on Wednesday with nearly 100 of its members and nine members of Congress in attendance. Made up of over 290 nonprofit organizations from the Chesapeake Bay region, the non-profit advocates maintaining or increasing spending on clean water programs.
"I think the Chesapeake delegation in Congress is just so passionate about this work, and they understand the benefits to their districts and the people that live there," Kristin Reilly, director of the coalition, told Capital News Service.
"I think that's also why there's such wide bipartisan support for these programs because they can actually see the benefits in their communities," Reilly added.
The Chesapeake Bay Program, which receives funding from the Environmental Protection Agency, was started in 1983, with its main efforts directed towards reducing pollution and restoring the bay's ecosystem.
The program encompasses six states that surround the bay as well as the District of Columbia, and its funding needs were at the forefront of the coalition's lobbying day. Over 70% of the program's funds are spent on projects in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, including planting trees, reducing runoff from farmland and boosting the crab and oyster populations.
The coalition highlighted the recent introduction of the America's Conservation Enhancement Reauthorization Act of 2024, which authorizes funding for various programs, including $93 million in funding for the EPA Chesapeake Bay Program for the 2025 fiscal year and $100 million for 2026 and beyond.
"This bill (the ACE Act) is going to get the bay on track," Rep. Dutch Ruppersberger (D-Md.) said. "Some of the things that these grants do, like sediment reduction, really make a difference in helping the Chesapeake Bay."
The coalition also is backing $15 million for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Watershed Investments for Landscape Defense program, which provides grants to local organizations in the Chesapeake region that focus on restoring or protecting wildlife habitats.
The coalition recognized Ruppersberger, Cardin and Rep. John Sarbanes (D-Md.) as "Chesapeake Champions" for their contributions to the restoration efforts throughout their careers.
Rep. David Trone (D-Md.), who is running for the U.S. Senate, said he plans to continue working to protect the bay if he wins the seat.
Pollutants need to be kept out of the bay and the efforts towards no-till farming have not been as successful in Pennsylvania and Virginia as in Maryland, Trone said. No-till farming is a technique used to grow crops without disturbing the soil.
"The environment is top of the list," Trone told CNS. "So the environment and the bay, that's the very very top of the list. If you don't get that right, nothing else matters."
After the luncheon, coalition members had scheduled 44 meetings with members of Congress, presenting letters from 169 organizations that endorsed the coalition's appropriations requests.
"We have to both maintain the momentum, but we also need to accelerate our efforts even further," Sen. Van Hollen (D-Md.) told CNS. "That means making sure that we protect and expand the resources that go to protect the bay from all the federal agencies."

title: Shark vs Seal: Scientists record one-of-a-kind deadly encounter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Shark vs Seal: Scientists record one-of-a-kind deadly encounter

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 267
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Seals and great white sharks have co-existed for over six million years and it is well-known they hunt seals.And now scientists are able to confirm they have been hunting them for millions of years.
A report was recently published in the journal Comptes Rendu Palevol by an international team that includes Calvert Marine Museum Curator of Paleontology Stephen J. Godfrey, Calvert Marine Museum Research Associate Paul R. Murdoch Jr. and St. Mary's College of Maryland's Victor J. Perez.
Until now, no great white shark tooth has ever been found embedded in a fossil seal bone, but the journal article reports on the discovery of the tip of a fossilized great white shark tooth embedded in a fossilized seal heel bone.
The unique two-for-one fossil was surface collected by Murdoch Jr. in Mosaic's South Fort Meade Mine in Florida. The seal bone originated from within the Bone Valley Member of the Peace River Formation of the Pliocene Epoch and is about 4.5 million years old.
The partial tooth is identified as having come from an Early Pliocene great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias). The discovery also represents the first great white shark tooth ever found embedded in any fossil bone, which may have come about as a result of active predation or scavenging.
The presence of the tooth in the seal's hind flipper suggests active pursuit and therefore active predation as opposed to scavenging.
Whatever the nature of the encounter, the seal did not survive given there is no evidence of healing on the fossilized seal bone.
To see the report, go to https://sciencepress.mnhn.fr/en/periodiques/comptes-rendus-palevol. For more information about the Calvert Marine Museum, go to www.calvertmarinemuseum.com.

title: House Environment and Transportation Committee hears proposed DAF storage bill
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
House Environment and Transportation Committee hears proposed DAF storage bill

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Del. Jeff Ghrist has withdrawn a bill that would have given local jurisdictions the authority to regulate the storage of dissolved air flotation by-products, or DAF residuals.Dissolved air flotation is a method used to process wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
On the Shore, much of the material generated from DAF comes from poultry processing plants, though some comes from industrial and wastewater treatment sludge.
In a letter to Del. Marc Korman (D-Montgomery), the chair of the Maryland House of Delegates Environment and Transportation Committee, Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) withdrew the bill he had introduced, House Bill 1404, and said he believed another bill, House Bill 991, would accomplish the same goals he is seeking if it is amended.
House Bill 991, which is sponsored by by Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery), would establish an industrial sludge utilization permit administered and enforced by the Department of the Environment.
In his letter, Ghrist said the current amended version of HB991 clearly "aims to give the necessary control to local governing bodies."
Ghrist took issue with how DAF is defined in this version of the bill. He said in the letter that DAF is being defined as an agricultural food processing residual, and as an agricultural operation, when it should be defined as industrial waste.
"This definition is important because any agricultural operation falls under the protection of the state's Right to Farm statute, and restrictions imposed by the local governing body could be challenged in court based on the protections granted by the Right to Farm," Ghrist said in the letter.
Ghrist said he he would like HB991 amended to separate DAF from other agricultural waste products "because it also includes other waste products that are not generated within the agricultural industry."
A hearing on HB991 was held Feb. 28, according to the Maryland General Assembly website. A second reading of the bill has not yet occurred. A hearing was held Tuesday for a cross-filed version of the bill, Senate Bill 1074, according to the General Assembly website. A second reading of that bill has not yet occurred either.
In an interview Thursday, Ghrist said he suspects the HB991 will get passed in the House before the 2024 legislative session ends on April 8. There has been a commitment from the Environment and Transportation Committee regarding this bill, he said, and when bills get support from the committee, they usually pass in the House.
In a Feb. 21 interview with the Star Democrat, Ghrist said he had introduced HB1404 to make sure that local governing bodies could put restrictions on the storage of DAF residuals "without any ambiguity." He said he wanted to ensure that if anybody decided to sue Caroline County, the case would not have any standing in court.
Caroline County Commissioners have been dealing with concerns regarding DAF storage since December. According to previous Star Democrat reporting, in late February, the commissioners voted to adopt four resolutions designed to give them time to study the issue of storing DAF residuals and other materials in the county.
The moratoriums address issues the County Commissioners learned about in December, when residents complained of possible illegal storage of DAF residuals.

title: Easter fun that doesn't end up in the landfill
author: Tamara Tsaturyan Food Drink Life
content:
Easter fun that doesn't end up in the landfill

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Tsaturyan Food Drink Life | Section: Entertainment 
 
 1037
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Spring has sprung, bunnies are hopping, but wait a minute — where has all the plastic gone? This time around, have Easter fun that leaves a mark on memories and not on the planet.What goes into creating memorable Easter fun? Plastic eggs and baskets, fake grass and candy wrappers probably aren't at the top of the list. If you're buying disposable plastic every year only to throw it away once Easter is over, then you might want to learn about alternative, fun and eco-friendly Easter festivities.
Say no to single-use plastic
For many Americans, spring flowers or warmer weather may not be the first signs of Easter's approach. Instead, your initial reminder about the upcoming holiday likely comes from the shelves of your local Target. As retailers begin stocking Easter-themed holiday items, you might feel tempted to pick up a bunch of cheap plastic eggs and Easter decorations while running other errands. It's hard to resist the allure of making your Easter egg hunt a little bit easier to plan.
Unfortunately, what begins as an impulse purchase often ends up in the landfill. Those plastic eggs, which look so tempting on display in stores, lose their appeal once the holiday is over. Many families may not have the space to store bulky Easter baskets or piles of crumpled plastic grass. Since most of that plastic can't be recycled, according to Nature World News, families simply throw it away.
With 81% of Americans celebrating Easter, according to Statista, those individual choices can add up quickly. UN experts are sounding the alarm about the toxic tidal wave of plastic, such as toys, bags and other products that end up contaminating the environment. In a recent statement, UN's David R. Boyd and Marcos Orellana warned that "the contribution of plastic pollution to climate change is alarming, yet often overlooked."
The good news is that it's possible to have beloved Easter festivities without all that waste. For many Christians, the real meaning of Easter isn't buying and discarding a jumble of single-use plastics. Instead, the holiday is a time to reflect upon core Christian values of sacrifice and simplicity.
Eco-friendly Easter activities for kids
With a little creativity and planning, you can introduce fun Easter activities that don't involve spending money on wasteful plastic products. Instead, hop into an Easter celebration that's kind to your wallet and the Earth. Here are some ideas to get you started.
Outdoor Easter scavenger hunt
In a twist on classic Easter egg hunts, don't send your kids out searching for plastic eggs. Instead, organize an outdoor Easter scavenger hunt with fun riddles as clues. Have meaningful prizes at the end of the hunt.
Easter baking
Ditch the individually wrapped Easter candies and bake some Easter treats together as a family. Cookies, wrapped in paper or stored in jars, are a great gift to share with loved ones.
Dyeing hard-boiled eggs
Did you know that dyeing real hard-boiled eggs is way more fun? It's easy to use natural food dyes, like onion skin or turmeric. And because these dyes are natural, you can eat the eggs as part of your Easter menu, so nothing goes to waste.
Gardening
Easter is all about celebrating new beginnings. Planting seeds or seedlings with kids is an engaging activity that is also environmentally friendly.
DIY-ing instead of buying
DIY instead of buying your Easter baskets this year. Egg cartons, old newspapers and magazines can all be used to make Easter baskets and decorations.
"One of our family's favorite activities to do on Easter is crafting," says Siobhan Alvarez-Borland of Mimosas and Motherhood. "From keepsake handprint or footprint crafts to utilizing found materials from an outdoor nature hunt to create a spring collage, this family crafting time has become one of our most treasured traditions."
If your kids are old enough, encourage them to get involved in planning and choosing eco-friendly options for Easter. This will not only help kids understand the importance of sustainability, but it's also a great way to get them excited about celebrating holidays in a way that doesn't damage the planet.
Tips for reducing waste during Easter celebrations
No matter how you celebrate Easter, there are lots of ways to reduce waste. Start by taking stock of what you already have. You may turn up a box of Easter decorations you didn't know you owned, avoiding the need to purchase something new. Or, consider connecting with other community members who are also celebrating Easter to swap supplies.
When you're putting together Easter baskets, don't forget about your local thrift store. Thrift stores often have a plethora of wicker baskets available at low prices. These higher-quality reusable baskets can be saved and re-used from year to year, avoiding waste. If you own a shredder or a pair of scissors, you can easily create your own recyclable paper grass — an alternative to plastic Easter grass.
Visit your local retailers to check out eco-friendly alternatives to Easter-themed plastic products. Recyclable paper eggs, which are great for decorating the house or an Easter egg hunt, are becoming increasingly available in stores. Also, use eco-friendly basket fillers, like tickets to zoos or museums, seed bombs and wooden puzzles.
The positive impact of eco-friendly Easter fun
Initially, a low-waste Easter might seem like added pressure during an already busy time of celebration planning. But, as you implement the tips suggested in this article, you might be surprised at how sustainability becomes less of a chore and more of an integral part of your family values. You'll quickly appreciate the liberating feeling of having less plastic waste cluttering up your home post-celebration.
Developing sustainable holiday traditions reduces waste and minimizes your family's environmental footprint. When you engage in eco-friendly activities it's an opportunity for family bonding while also setting a great example for children. Avoiding consumerism on Easter is the perfect way to be grateful for what you already have, placing the focus firmly on Easter's true meaning.
Before you know it, as your kids enjoy an outdoor Easter scavenger hunt, you'll be hunting for more ways to keep your family's life eco-friendly beyond Easter — and the planet will thank you for it.
Tamara Tsaturyan is the owner and writer of Thriving In Parenting, a website focused on providing simple tips for busy parents — easy and healthy recipes, home decor and organization ideas and all things parenting.

title: Maryland debates “local” wind farm, way offshore
author: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service
content:
Maryland debates “local” wind farm, way offshore

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service | Section: General Assembly 
 
 644
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland wants to expand its use of renewable energy by encouraging local projects like wind turbines.But one company's plan to build windmills in waters off the coast is running into trouble this session in the General Assembly, where lawmakers worry about giving their economic support to a project that isn't exactly local.
The proposed project would be built off the coast of Virginia Beach — close by, but technically outside Maryland waters.
One lawmaker wants to help the company building it, Avangrid Renewables, by making a wording change in a Maryland law that defines who is eligible to sell energy credits to the state. Her bill would expand the current law to let Maryland buy and sell energy credits from a company whose planned wind turbines are closer to the shores of Virginia and North Carolina.
The measure is "a crucial step towards removing obstacles to offshore wind development in Maryland," said Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City), who is sponsoring the measure. "This bill has the potential to expedite the state's transition to renewable energy."
But when the General Assembly bought into a set of ambitious renewable energy goals last year, they did so partly because advocates had convinced them they would be beneficial to the local economy. Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George's) argues that those local economic benefits would not materialize for Marylanders if the wind farms were built in other states.
"We want to have the power, of course — we want to have the renewable energy," Augustine told Capital News Service. "But we also want to have that economic benefit that's associated with the development… stay here."
The bill follows last year's POWER Act, which established Maryland's goal of procuring 8.5 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2031, dramatically increasing the state's previous goal.
Renewable energy generators like Avangrid said this bill could help the state meet its goal by supporting the construction of more than one local offshore wind project on the PJM grid, a power grid that connects several states, including Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Maryland. Maryland's pledge of support as a future energy credit buyer would help advance any project.
"This lease area that we're talking about is gigantic," said Ken Kimmell, Avangrid's vice president of development for offshore wind. "So it's quite possible that the lease area could support a project for Maryland and also a project for Virginia."
Both states would benefit environmentally and economically, Kimmell said. There are proposed "marshaling ports" in Baltimore where the wind turbine's parts would be staged for installation, he said. In addition, the use of union laborers at these ports would benefit Maryland, Kimmell added.
Other lawmakers are not yet convinced. Some are worried about the negative impacts of offshore wind in general and have concerns about the costs of expanding these initiatives.
Ocean City residents have voiced concerns about offshore wind's impact on the tourism industry, said Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Worcester and Wicomico). She has raised concerns about the potential impact on military training and exercises in the area, as well as fishing and marine life.
"There was an expert that testified at the congressional hearing in Ocean City that talked about the impact of the noise on the whales . . . whether it's the drilling of the turbines or whether it's the sound from the turbines themselves that would cause harm to the whales and other marine life," she said. "You also have then whether the project even makes sense from a cost perspective."
Augustine is also concerned that it doesn't make sense. "How in the world does something landing in North Carolina benefit Maryland?" he asked in the bill hearing last week.
Lawmakers are open to other legislation this session that would propel the state further toward its renewable energy goals.
But legislators still aren't big fans of this particular effort. And with time running out before a crucial session deadline, the bill may stall for now.

title: Boy Scouts build barn owl boxes for Blackwater
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Boy Scouts build barn owl boxes for Blackwater

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Boy Scout Troop 209 spent part of a weekend busy at Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge mounting barn owl boxes and laying down gravel.The scouts, with the help of their parents and Blackwater's biologists, replaced two barn owl boxes and added an extra box to the refuge on Feb. 25. They also added more gravel to a ramp to level it and improve accessibility to a photo blind located off Wildlife Drive.
Boy Scout Keegan Hulett, 14, is on his way to becoming an Eagle Scout, and this project is a step toward that achievement.
He said the entire experience was "very fun."
Along with his fellow Scouts, Hulett was surprised about how long the owl boxes will last on the refuge.
"We thought it would last only two or three years," he said, "but apparently, it'll be set for the next 15 years."
Blackwater Wildlife biologist Holly Keepers said successful nesting rates have been decreasing for barn owls.
"By having these structures put up, we're giving the barn owls more options," she said. "And they're able to hopefully — in the future — have more nestlings and more babies than before."
Not only did the Scouts mount the boxes on the refuge, but they also built them.
Hulett's mother, Jeannie VanDyke, said the boys spent an entire Saturday at her dad's house building the barn owl boxes according to the specs that Blackwater sent them.
Keepers said the refuge really appreciates community service projects like these.
"We love projects like these at the refuge," she said. "But unfortunately it takes a lot of time and money, and wood is very expensive now. So having these projects, especially with people being able to come out and enjoy the day on the refuge, it was really, really nice."
Keepers said the new boxes are bigger and better than before.
The work to the photo blind ramp was an addition to the owl box project.
"Most (Boy Scout) troops are pretty large," VanDyke said. "So when Keegan went to the Scout board to tell them about the project that needed to be done, they weren't sure if it was enough for an Eagle project. So Keegan asked Blackwater if there was anything else the boys could do in addition to that."
Hulett encouraged others to consider becoming a Scout.
"Anyone who's looking to go into the Boy Scouts, you should definitely consider it," he said. "It's really fun."

title: Dire need of conservation
author: Staff Writer
content:
Dire need of conservation

 March 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 301
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's a hard truth we must accept when it comes to Chesapeake stripers. There will be no future for striped bass, or the charter captains and watermen who rely on them, if we stick with the status quo.Striped bass are key to Maryland's ecosystem and economy, especially in places like Kent County, as described in Will Bontrager's recent article. Which is why new regulations adopted by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) are so important.
While fishermen may still be catching trophy stripers, there are very few juvenile striped bass to replace them. Juvenile striped bass numbers in Maryland have been far below average for the past five years. Bontrager's article notes this, stating, "In October 2023, according to the DNR, the results of the annual juvenile striped bass survey found the worst recruitment in Maryland since 1957."
The species is in dire need of conservation and keeping populations at a sustainable level will require long-term, cooperative solutions.
ASMFC reports that striped bass removals, which include harvested fish and catch and release mortality, were up 33 percent in 2022. Unsustainable fishing levels, paired with reproductive failure, habitat loss and climate change, have left the striped bass population extremely vulnerable.
It is ASMFC's responsibility to act on these very concerning losses, and economic impacts are carefully considered as part of their fisheries management plan.
After the 1985 moratorium, the species was able to rebound relatively quickly. Striped bass, and those who value them, won't have that luxury this time with the added stress of increased habitat loss and climate change. Those stressors, paired with invasive predators like blue catfish, will make it extremely difficult for the species to recover. If we want to preserve the fate of striped bass, charter boats, and watermen, we need action now and foresight for the future.
ALLISON COLDEN

title: EPA announces historic funding for Chesapeake Bay restoration
author: BRENNAN STEWART Capital News Service
content:
EPA announces historic funding for Chesapeake Bay restoration

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BRENNAN STEWART Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ARLINGTON, Va. — The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced Wednesday that $206 million in funding will be allocated towards projects aimed at continuing the restoration of the Chesapeake Bay.The historic levels of funding reflect the Biden administration's increased investments in environmental programs and infrastructure projects.
"For a long time, the EPA's budget has been so small, roughly about $10 billion a year," EPA Assistant Deputy Administrator Mark Rupp said during a ceremony at the recently-built Lubber Run Community Center here. "Between the
Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the Inflation Reduction Act, there's now over $100 billion flowing through our agency, and it really has been a game changer."
With $96 million of the funds coming from President Joe Biden's so-called "Investing in America" agenda alone, the announcement marked the largest single contribution to the Chesapeake Bay Program in its 41-year history.
Maryland is expected to receive over $14 million from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation's share of the funds, which in turn makes up 40 individual grant projects.
Grant recipients include the Baltimore Tree Trust, which plans to educate city residents about planting trees in their communities.
The Severn River Association will be another recipient. The organization intends to increase and improve stormwater treatment practices on the Severn River, which flows into the Chesapeake Bay in Annapolis.
"Agendas matter, elected officials matter, vision matters," Rep. Gerry Connolly (D-Virginia) said. "For the sake of the country, thank God we have the 117th Congress and Joe Biden to sign those bills into law."
Attending the ceremony were not only federal officials and members of Congress but also legislators from state and local governments around the Chesapeake Bay.
Libby Garvey, chair of the Arlington County Board, said funds are going to be used in her community on a small tributary called Grandma's Creek.
"(The Grandma's Creek project) is a great example of community involvement and advocacy for a beloved neighborhood stream," Garvey said. "This project is going to propose the installation of rain gardens to better manage stormwater and increase the protection of the creek."
In addition to rain gardens, the Arlington community will also have the opportunity to participate in organized tree plantings and pop-up educational events centered around nature, Garvey said. The funds for these projects will be derived from the Small Watershed Grants Program, one of three grant programs administered by the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, which is to receive $193 million of the $206 million.
The NFWF already has announced it will be giving $1 million to farmers in Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia, with the intention of implementing high-priority conservation practices that improve water quality.
"There are 40,000 farms in Pennsylvania, and many of them contribute nutrients and sediment to the bay," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia) said. "So anything we can do to get Pennsylvania on board with Maryland, Virginia and Delaware will be incredibly important."
The Chesapeake Bay Trust, another non-profit grant-making organization, will receive the remaining $13 million from the EPA. The trust will use the money to assist local organizations involved with improving the bay.
This could include providing operational infrastructure like computers and other hardware, or funding employee training and professional development sessions.
"We have to do better on agricultural runoff, and we have to do better on stormwater runoff. We do well on sewage treatment and on other point source pollution," Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Virginia) told Capital News Service. "This $200 million is going to be heavily focused on grants that focus on non-point sources, and we should continue to see significant improvements."

title: Nature Notes
author: JAY FALSTAD Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Nature Notes

 April 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JAY FALSTAD Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Nature Notes 
 
 684
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Turtles will soon be on the move — you can help them.With warmer temperatures just around the corner, many of the Eastern Shore's turtle species will soon be on the move. Unlike other animals that hibernate during winter months, reptiles and amphibians brumate, and when they wake up from their brumation period, they start to move in search of food, a place to warm up, search for new mates, new territory and new nesting sites.
Maryland's Eastern Shore holds 14 of Maryland's 19 turtle species. Turtles are classified as aquatic, semi-aquatic or terrestrial. Only the Box Turtle is considered a full-time terrestrial, spending its entire life on land.
Here on the Eastern Shore, as soon as temperatures break the 50 degree mark, turtle activity increases. As turtles emerge from winter brumation sites, they can be seen basking in the sun to warm themselves. Turtles are ectothermic (cold-blooded) and their activities and movements are determined by the surrounding temperature. By mid-April, it's not uncommon to see turtles moving about, sometimes crossing roadways.
Sadly, many turtle species are struck by vehicles as they try to cross roads. Beyond the threat of vehicle strikes, turtles are also threatened by climate change, shoreline armoring (like riprap), rising sea levels, and poaching.
So why do Turtles cross the road? Most turtles cross roadways in search of nesting sites, so ensuring their safe passage is crucial in supporting the turtle's future. While most turtles are aquatic or semi-aquatic, they all need higher and drier ground to lay their eggs.
If you see a turtle crossing a roadway, you can help, but it's important to know a few things, take a few precautions, and most importantly, be safe.
First, if you can help a roadside turtle, it's important that you help turtles cross in the direction they're going. Smaller turtles like Box Turtles or Sliders, can usually be helped easily enough, just be cautious. Never relocate turtles to different regions and never keep them as pets. According to Maryland DNR Herptologist, Beth Schlimm, "…all turtles, especially Box Turtles, have a limited range and spend their entire lives in a pretty small area. If a turtle is moved to a new location, it may attempt to navigate back to their original territory, increasing the chances of being harmed or killed." It's ok to help turtles cross the road, but never relocate them to unfamiliar surroundings and always be careful.
Helping Snapping Turtles cross roadways requires a little extra care. Snappers have sharp claws, a nasty bite, and quick reflexes, so be cautious! They also will hold in place when they feel threatened. If you want to attempt to move a Snapping Turtle, it's best to use gloves and hold the turtle on the backsides of its shell. Never move or lift a Snapping Turtle by its tail. Doing so can cause major skeletal damage to the turtle. There are online videos on how best to move Snapping Turtles.
Turtles will typically lay their eggs between June and September. If you find a turtle digging a hole and depositing eggs, it's best to observe from a distance, but do not disturb or touch a nesting turtle. All turtles, even aquatic turtles, lay their eggs on land. They search out higher ground away from water. Wet turtle eggs result in poor incubation and low survival rates. Homeowners will sometimes find turtles laying their eggs in garden mulch or sandy soils. The incubation period for most turtle eggs is about 60 days.
For shoreline residents and recreational crabbers who have crab pots hanging on their piers, make sure your crab pots have a Crab Pot Turtle Reduction device. Maryland DNR officers will be on the look-out making sure crab traps are in compliance. These devices are necessary to prevent air breathing turtles from drowning in crab traps.
Turtles are an important part of Maryland's diverse ecosystem and we can all do a better job of helping our turtle species. The turtle's future is dependent on us. To learn more about Maryland's turtles, search Maryland Turtles in your web browser.
Jay Falstad is a Maryland Master Naturalist and Executive Director of the Queen Anne's Conservation Association.

title: Fishery Association takes limit to court
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Fishery Association takes limit to court

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 866
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GRASONVILLE — Chairman of Delmarva Fisheries Association Rob Newberry is opposing a single-limit fish-per-person rule set by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, or ASMFA, slated to take effect May 1. In an effort to protect the interests of those watermen he represents, he's taking the issue to court.Instead of allowing two rockfish per person as in times past, regulations state only one can be caught this year.
The new rules reduce the recreational catch limit on striped bass from two bass at 19 to 31 inches per person to one fish at 19 to 24 inches per person.
The position of DNR and ASMFC is that these emergency actions are needed, and the tighter striped bass fishing regulations are in response to ongoing population decline and rock-bottom reproduction.
In October 2023, according to the DNR, the results of the annual juvenile striped bass survey found the worst recruitment in Maryland since 1957.
The ASMFA argues the regulations will help reduce fishing-related mortality.
Newberry, a captain himself, said the measures will just hurt the fishing industry. And he's certainly not alone in this stance.
The Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian expressed his disapproval of the regulations during the commission's session on March 5.
"In 2022, we had $72 million in visitor spending, so this is very detrimental to Kent County. This is going to affect the lodging, restaurants...any and all of them," he said.
"Quite frankly, it's going to be a gut punch to the county. We're speaking out against it," Fithian said.
In an interview, Newberry, building on the commissioner's statements, said the regulations won't just affect the charter boat industry, but commercial and recreational fishermen throughout the entire state.
It prompted him, as well as commercial waterman Brian Nesspor; Brian Hardman, the president of the Maryland Charter Boat Association; and Kenneth Jeffries, vice president of the Upper Bay Charter Captains Association, to file a formal lawsuit challenging the ASMFC's mandate.
At Newberry's latest meeting Saturday, March 30, at the Grasonville VFW, he updated the roughly 100 in attendance on what happens next.
Hardman also spoke, as well as their attorney James Butera of Meeks, Butera and Israel.
Newberry lamented that he sent out invitations to all 146 legislators, as well as the governor and secretary of agriculture, inviting them to the meeting, but none showed up.
He also sent invitations out to all the Eastern Shore Delegates. Delegate Jay Jacobs and Maryland State Senator Stephen Hershey were in attendance.
However, there is statewide support for their case, Newberry noted, coming from The Maryland Rural County Coalition, who claims the one-fish policy will have an adverse affect on Maryland's economy.
The memorandum supporting Newberry's claims indicate they filed their complaint regarding "ASMFC's promulgation on January 24, 2024 of drastic and unwarranted limitations on commercial and recreational fishing for Atlantic Striped Bass in the coastal Atlantic Ocean and, in particular, the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries."
Cutting through some of the legal terminology, Newberry summed it up as the ASMFC acted outside the bounds of the U.S. and the Maryland Constitution.
"They (ASMFC) promulgated regulations directly in violation of that," Newberry said.
He said he's hopeful to have the new rules overturned, based on the crowd at meetings and the overwhelming support he said his efforts have received from the counties.
Newberry has faced what he described as a naysayer, Russell Dize, the vice president of Maryland Watermen's Association. Newberry said Dize claimed this lawsuit was a "waste of time and resources."
There's more opposition as well, including that of the Bay Foundation and the Coastal Conservation Association.
Newberry was adamant when he said he "doesn't care" what they think.
And even more so, Newberry said, the optics are not in the favor of the ASMFC when describing the process in which the regulations were first enacted.
He explained. The ASMFC is composed of three deciding bodies: representatives of the governor's office, representatives from the Department of Natural Resources and representatives for the legislative body headed by Speaker Pro Tempore Delegate Dana Stein, his proxy being David Sikorski, executive director of the Coastal Conservation Association.
The only one initially voting for the stricter regulations was within Stein's body, Newberry said. Nobody from the Department of Natural Resources nor the governors office was for the new mandate.
According to Newberry, Sikorski lobbied for the one-fish rule to the ASMFC commission, influencing them.
This doesn't sit right with Newberry, who is calling for the Eastern Shore delegation and the entire legislative body to clarify its position.
He wants them to be clear so Marylanders will understand who they elected into office.
"Right now, the whole thing looks like the legislative body is responsible for putting Marylanders out of work," Newberry said.
He and others filed the lawsuit in federal court on March 8. On March 22, they signed a memorandum of understanding.
The hearing will be held on April 12, 11 a.m. at the federal court building in Baltimore concerning the complaint. Moving forward, a trial date will be set for April 26.
ASMFC is required to have their answer to the complaint by April 5 and the plaintiffs response to that by April 9.
In his years of defending watermen's issues Newberry said this effort is one of the larger ones he has taken on.
"This is rather important," Newberry noted. "It's our economy we're taking about. Our livelihood."

title: Listening at the Talbot County Free Library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Listening at the Talbot County Free Library

 April 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 935
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We live on a two and a half acre wooded lot. The northern end of the property is marked by a ridge that stands some fifty feet above sea level, an elevation seldom encountered in Talbot County. From there, the ground descends slowly but surely toward the southern boundary, the wetlands bordering the Choptank River.When asked if we have waterfront property, we always smile and say, "No, but it is at least marsh-front."
About halfway down the property, two streambeds enter our lot, one running along its eastern edge, and the other its western. The peaty floors of the valleys channeling these streams form two elongated wetlands. Our house sits on the spit of high ground separating the two valleys. I like to sit out on the southern end of this peninsula and look out over the spot where the two streams and their valleys converge into a single larger wetland.
As a result of its topography, our small piece of land is blessed with a number of different habitats: a mixed upland forest of loblolly, oak, beech and hickory, with a darker understory of holly; a middle elevation consisting of more holly, tall and short bush blueberry, mountain laurel, sassafras, black and sweet gum, and the occasional, cherished, crane fly orchid; and then, further down, at the lowest elevation, wetlands comprised of bay magnolia, shad bush, pinxter azalea, ironwood, green ash, maple, spice bush, fern, wild rice and swamp iris. In the summer the foliage becomes jungle-thick, blocking our view of the distant river, but we don't mind: the fragrances are heavenly.
When I sit out on the point overlooking the confluence of our two streambeds, I like to close my eyes and try to identify the sounds happening around me. In addition to all the bird calls (147 species and counting), these may include the seesawing, rasping song of a gray squirrel, the drawn-out, rubbery chupting of leopard frogs, the high-pitched yodeling of a dog fox, the double-stomp and snort of a white-tailed deer or the rustling in the leaf litter that signals the presence of a snake or mouse.
Once I heard a raccoon give a most un-raccoon-like call, a call which — had I not watched the raccoon make it — I would have attributed to a coyote.
On another occasion, way off to the west of me, I began hearing a low whisper, like the noise air makes when it leaks slowly from a puncture. Focusing on the gentle hissing noise, I realized its decibel level was growing second-by-second, becoming now the sound of a distant breeze, now that of a crowd of people speaking just beyond the range of understanding.
The crescendo reached its peak when a great horned owl burst from the trees on my right pursued by a swirling comet's tail of angry complaining chickadees, titmice and nuthatches.
I'm reading a wonderful book about sound just now, David George Haskell's "Sounds Wild and Broken," which I checked out through the consortium of libraries that allows Talbot County Free Library card members to check out books, DVDs and audiobooks from any library on the Eastern Shore.
As with all good science books, Haskell's has enriched my enjoyment of the natural world. Now, when I sit out there at the end of the high ground and notice the surface of the water at the foot of our point roiling with small spawning fish, a part of me thinks that, instead of calling them banded killifish or golden shiners, I should refer to them as brother or sister fish. For Haskell has taught me that each of us carries within us the inheritance of their and our marine ancestors.
When the first fishes crawled up out of the sea to become terrestrial animals, they carried with them, like the aqualungs we use to return to the sea, a portion of their watery environment. Thanks to the extraordinary organ known as skin, each of us still carries a semblance of that ocean environment within us; we remain, in essence, walking containers of our ancestors' liquid world.
We humans owe our ability to hear to three small bones in our inner ears, one of which began its evolutionary journey as part of a fish ancestor's gills. These bones transmit sound vibrations from the outside world to the ears' nerve center, the cochlea, a snail-like organ filled with, yet again, a sea-like liquid. Basically, when we sit by the fire and listen to a Bach toccata, we listen to it using ocean water and fish bones.
Twenty-eight years ago, shortly after we moved into our house, I was sitting out on the point listening to all the birdsong incited by the first warm day of spring when I heard a call unlike any I had ever heard before.
Up until that point, I had lived most of my life in urban settings, so I was eager to identify the more natural sounds belonging to the landscape around our new home. I turned my chair toward the noise, which seemed to be coming from beyond the woods on the other side of the valley east of me, and focused on it. It was a high-pitched call, like the laughter of a woodpecker but less harsh, and there seemed to be more than one animal producing it.
After a moment's perplexity, I smiled. On a property upriver of us, two or three little girls were playing a game, perhaps jump-rope, their squeals of delight floating down to me on the moist, fragrant early-spring air. For the first time in my life I had heard human voices as animals must hear them: strange and wondrous, alien and alive.

title: How will dogs, cats, birds, livestock and wild animals react to the total solar eclipse?
author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
content:
How will dogs, cats, birds, livestock and wild animals react to the total solar eclipse?

 April 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor | Section: Eclipse 
 
 588
 Words 

 Read News Document

 All eyes will be to the sky for Monday's total solar eclipse when the moon will darken the sun bringing with it daytime darkness.But there is also interest in how animals — from family dogs and house cats to birds and other wild creatures — react to the eclipse across the U.S.
Jacob Dykes, a wildlife specialist and assistant professor at the Texas A&M University in Corpus Christi, will be keeping tabs on how animals react to the eclipse.
"Even among members of the same species, there is quite a lot of variation in how animals respond," said Dykes, who studies animal behaviors. "It may be down to the individual. Some animals respond and some don't. Right now, it's a question that nobody seems to have a complete answer to."
The Texas A&M researcher said animals at a zoo in South Carolina showed varying reactions to an eclipse in 2017 — including some that began nighttime preparations, some that looked to the sky and others who displayed signs of anxiety or unusual activities.
"Researchers saw giraffes suddenly start running around their pen," Dykes said. "Some of the male gorillas became more aggressive. These were some of the anxiety behaviors."
"For birds, they would suddenly go to nest and then a few minutes later, when the sun came back out, they would seem to start their day all over again," he said. "There's no telling what's running through these critters' minds when, suddenly midday, the sky goes dark. Their environment is always having an influence, whether through rain, temperature, wind speed, the amount of sunlight or the length of day. Wildlife are deeply in tune with their surroundings."
Researchers from other universities as well as students and teachers from high schools will also be studying animal and wildlife behaviors.
That includes a contingent from North Carolina State University who will be part of a research effort at the Fort Worth Zoo in Texas during the April 8 eclipse.
Adam Hartstone-Rose, a biology professor at North Carolina State, was also at the Riverbanks Zoo and Garden in Columbia, South Carolina in 2017.
He's excited for the 2024 total solar eclipse to see how animals react.
The researchers welcome input from others who see how farm animals, dogs and cats and other wildlife react during the cosmic happening.
"We're interested not only in figuring out which animals react to the eclipse and how, but (to) what extent of totality is necessary to cause a reaction," Hartsone-Rose said.
"We're really excited about getting data from people that might be at farms or cattle ranches," he said. "We're hoping that people will go out into the woods and see what squirrels, deer and birds are doing. And I'm really excited about people just observing their pets in their backyard."
The eclipse will be visible to varying degrees across the U.S. with a path of totality where the moon will completely darken the sun for three to four minutes stretching from Texas and Oklahoma and into Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, upstate New York and New England.
Overcast conditions and stormy weather could impact how visible the eclipse is in parts of the country — including Texas and Ohio.
It will be the biggest eclipse in the U.S. since 1806 and there will not be another similar event until 2044.
Zoos — especially those in or near the totality path of the eclipse — will also be hosting special events for visitors Monday. That includes ones in Indianapolis, Toledo, Ohio, St. Louis and throughout Texas.
The eclipse comes after a 4.8 magnitude earthquake hit Friday in New Jersey near New York City.

title: Maryland legislation regulating DAF storage passes through General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Maryland legislation regulating DAF storage passes through General Assembly

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: General Assembly 
 
 729
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Saturday, Maryland lawmakers voted to pass a bipartisan bill to address the state's authority to regulate the storage of dissolved air flotation byproducts, or DAF residuals.If signed into law, this would be a victory for some residents of Caroline Country, who have been advocating for more regulations concerning DAF storage. The bill is currently awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
Dissolved air flotation is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
On the Shore, much of the material generated from DAF comes from poultry processing plants, though some comes from industrial and wastewater treatment sludge.
The bill refers to the material as "food processing residuals," which it defines as "an organic material that is generated by processing agricultural commodities for human or animal consumption."
According to a 2023 study by the University of Maryland, more than half of the industrial sludge land applied in Maryland in recent years came from other states. In Maryland, it is an approved soil amendment or fertilizer.
Alan Girard, Maryland advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, said that if not properly regulated, overapplication and mishandling of this material could risk local water quality and Bay health.
"Improper handling and application of industrial sludge cause it to spill and run off directory into our local waterways and ultimately into the Chesapeake Bay," Girard said. "It's also a major concern for the Marylanders living near these sludge application and storage sites that drink well water and live off the land."
The state legislation will close a loophole in state oversight and keep Maryland on par with neighboring states, according to a press release by the Chesapeake Bay Foundation.
The bill, House Bill 991, and its paired Senate bill, 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
Maryland does not currently require a permit for DAF residuals.
If the new legislation is signed into law, counties will still be able to issue their own regulations when it comes to utilizing food processing residuals, though they must comply with state regulations.
HB 991 and SB1074 will do the following:
Requiring a utilization permit for the use, storage and hauling of food processing residuals in the state.Ensuring local governments issue all necessary approvals before someone can utilize food processing residuals.Authorizing the Maryland Department of Agriculture to enter and inspect any site where food processing residuals is used.Increase penalties for users who willfully violate Maryland's nutrient management regulations.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
In mid-December, residents complained to the Caroline County Commissioners about the odor and flies emanating from a DAF storage pit near Greensboro and about their fear of groundwater contamination and waterways.
"Caroline County has no authority to prohibit the application of DAF to farmland and the MDA and MDE do not regulate the storage of DAF residuals; therefore, Caroline County is not preempted by the State regarding the storage of DAF residuals," Daniel Fox, deputy county administrator, said.
Subsequent inquiries and investigation by county staff resulted in a proposed moratorium of DAF residual storage in the county, prompting hundreds of residents to attend a Jan. 23 public hearing in Denton.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
The moratoriums aimed to buy the county more time to decide how it wanted to regulate the materials. In the meantime, state legislators worked to pass the House and Senate bills through the General Assembly.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery), Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation at the state level.
"It's a bill that will hopefully give us some more control over where the material is stored, which is what we're looking for," Porter said at a meeting of the Caroline County Commissioners April 9. "It does address transportation, and it does address application through the nutrient management plan, which we were interested in anyway."
Reporter Maggie Trovato contributed to this report.

title: Wild turkey numbers are falling in some parts of the U.S. – the main reason may be habitat loss
author: Marcus Lashley and William Gulsby The Conversation
content:
Wild turkey numbers are falling in some parts of the U.S. – the main reason may be habitat loss

 April 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marcus Lashley and William Gulsby The Conversation | Section: Environment 
 
 1264
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Birdsong is a welcome sign of spring, but robins and cardinals aren't the only birds showing off for breeding season. In many parts of North America, you're likely to encounter male wild turkeys, puffed up like beach balls and with their tails fanned out, aggressively strutting through woods and parks or stopping traffic on your street.Wild turkeys were abundant across North America when European settlers arrived. But people killed them indiscriminately year-round — sometimes for their meat and feathers, but settlers also took turkey eggs from nests and poisoned adult turkeys to keep them from damaging crops. Thanks to this unregulated killing and habitat loss, by 1900 wild turkeys had disappeared from much of their historical range.
Turkey populations gradually recovered over the 20th century, aided by regulation, conservation funding and state restoration programs. By the early 2000s, they could be found in Mexico, Canada and every U.S. state except Alaska.
Now, however, the trend appears to be reversing in some areas. In a 2021 study, eight out of 30 states surveyed reported that turkey populations declined from 2014 to 2019, with some of the sharpest decreases in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana and Oklahoma.
Turkey numbers increased in 14 states, mainly in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic. But even in many of those states, populations were down from historic peaks in the early 2000s. Another study in 2023 reported that turkey populations in the eastern half of the U.S. were declining by about 9% yearly, based on data from the past 50 years.
We are wildlife ecologists working to determine why turkey populations are shrinking in portions of their range. This is a classic challenge in ecology: Many factors could be at play, and it takes careful analysis to untangle them and figure out whether each trend is a cause or symptom — or just irrelevant.
We created the Wild Turkey Science podcast to make peer-reviewed science accessible to the public and provide a platform for turkey researchers and biologists to discuss their work. So far, we have reviewed numerous studies and interviewed scientists from more than a dozen states. Here are some hypotheses that have emerged:
Fewer open spaces
While turkeys may appear at home in urban areas, their habitat is open forest — areas with sparse trees that allow near-full sunlight to reach herbaceous plants at ground level. Most uplands, or elevated areas, in the eastern U.S. historically were this type of dry-adapted woodland, savanna and grassland complex.
In 1792, naturalist William Bartram described the eastern U.S. as "Grande Savane," or big savanna, a landscape with abundant wild turkeys. Traveling in Florida, Bartram wrote:
"I was awakened, in the morning early, by the cheering converse of the wild turkey cocks saluting each other from the sun-brightened tops of the lofty cypress and magnolia. They begin at early dawn, and continue till sunrise. The high forests ring with the noise of these social sentinels, the watchword being caught and repeated, from one to another, for hundreds of miles around, insomuch that the whole country is, for an hour or more, in an universal shout."
Today, very little woodland or savanna remains in the U.S. Most of it has been cleared for development, farming or livestock grazing. The open spaces that are left often are not suitable for wild turkeys: They need a well-developed layer of vegetation at ground level that includes mainly wild flowers, native grasses and young shrubs and trees to provide cover for nesting and raising their young.
Very few of the remaining lands suitable for wild turkeys are managed using frequent, low-intensity prescribed fire, which creates and maintains a mosaic of open forest and grassland by continually setting back growth of trees, shrubs and vines. Suppressing fire in these forests across the eastern U.S. allows them to change from open forest dominated by fire-adapted grasses and wildflowers to closed forests with dense canopies, creating shady, moist conditions with minimal vegetation near ground level.
Turkeys can persist in these denser, shaded forests, but they don't reproduce as successfully, and fewer of their young survive. The lack of ground vegetation makes it hard for hens to hide their nests, and it limits food supplies for young turkey poults.
This isn't just a problem for wild turkeys. Over the past 50 years, populations of bird species that live in open forests and grasslands have fallen by more than 50%. Grasslands and savannas support hundreds of other wild species as well, many of which are declining.
The roles of food, predators and hunting
Scientists have proposed other explanations for turkey declines, but many of these hypotheses are at least partly habitat issues.
For example, blame is often placed on more abundant predators that eat turkey eggs, such as raccoons and opossums. But these predators probably are more abundant in part due to changes in turkey habitat.
For example, a 2024 study found that a range of mammals that eat turkey eggs were observed 70% of the time when prescribed burning was not used, but were observed less than 10% of the time in open forests where planned burns were conducted biannually. This suggests that prescribed fire across the wild turkey's range creates an environment that's more favorable for turkeys than for their predators.
Some observers have suggested that turkeys may be so abundant that the landscape can't support their current population, so now they are declining to a more sustainable level. If turkey habitat remained stable, we would expect to see their numbers go up and down naturally, but their average abundance over time would remain the same. Instead, turkey numbers appear to be slowly but steadily falling in many areas — perhaps signaling that habitat availability is declining along with turkey populations.
What about food supplies? Young turkeys feed on insects, so insect declines may explain some observed changes in turkey populations. According to one calculation, land-dwelling bird species that depend on insects as food have declined by 2.9 billion individuals over the past 50 years, while those species that don't have gained by 26.2 million individuals.
Insect losses could explain why fewer turkeys are surviving to adulthood, but insects depend on plants, so this shift is likely also linked to habitat changes. And where land is managed to promote native flowers and grasses, there also are abundant pollinators, ants, grasshoppers and spiders that turkeys relish.
Lastly, some observers have proposed that the timing of hunting could be affecting turkey reproduction. However, a recent study in Tennessee found that this was not the case. Another recent study showed that hunters in the Southeast were harvesting about the same share of male turkeys as when turkey populations were growing rapidly. If current turkey harvest rates are unsustainable, the explanation is likely that wild turkey productivity has declined for other reasons, such as habitat.
Creating space for turkeys
Land owners can help by managing for native grasses and wildflowers on their property, which will provide breeding habitat for turkeys. We have produced podcast episodes that discuss which plants are valuable to turkeys and other wildlife, and how to promote and maintain plants that are turkey-friendly.
People who don't own land can support state and local efforts to restore wildlife, contribute to local wildlife conservation groups and buy hunting licenses, which help to fund wildlife management programs. With the right conditions, this iconic North American species could thrive yet again.

title: Lives depend on effective shoreland protections
author: ELLE HOGAN
content:
Lives depend on effective shoreland protections

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ELLE HOGAN | Section: Columns 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Have you ever taken a sip of water, a taste of food or a breath of air and wondered if it was safe for your health and the environment? As a local who grew up on the Chesapeake Bay, I have watched firsthand as the water quality has worsened, water levels have risen and temperatures have skyrocketed.From swimming in pools instead of the Miles River to rarely seeing tubes or water skis on the water anymore, I always wondered what was causing such detriment to our water. Beyond the vast beauty and productivity of farmlands lining the shores of the Chesapeake Bay, the root cause of water pollution in the bay is harmful nutrients sourced from agricultural farm runoff.
Agricultural runoff is the leading cause of water pollution in the United States, threatening our water, food and air quality. The truth is, we are still not doing enough without effective policies to prevent our water quality from worsening, as bay water continues to threaten human health and environmental safety.
Without a shoreland protection policy to safeguard this issue, this problem is only progressing further, and water quality improvement goals are capable of being met. This environmental issue requires immediate attention because the current rate of detriment polluting the Chesapeake Bay water that we boat on, fish, crab, and oyster and hope to swim in and drink from safely is causing more harm than good for society.
Excess nutrients from farm runoff in the Chesapeake Bay have long-lasting effects: killing marine life, polluting swimming areas and drinking water, flooding properties and homes, and causing many health problems. These dangers also harshly target low-income and minority communities, who often experience disproportionate harm from pollution and other
environmental threats. The Chesapeake Bay Foundation's annual water quality report cards well document the extent of the bay's problems and current conditions, which are evidently not improving. Strict legislative change must be made because a safe environment, clean water and clean air are rights that need to be shared and fought for when threatened.
In order to create accurate and involuntary change, the Chesapeake Bay bordering states need to implement a shoreland zoning policy to enforce the protection of bay water quality from the threats of agricultural runoff. In environmentally unique yet critical areas like the Chesapeake Bay, the government must fund efforts to protect these crucial, indeed life and death, natural assets.
Farmers cannot and should not be burdened by the costs of such programs. Citizens have a constitutional right to a dependable food supply, safe water and clean air, which requires the government to legislate and fund these efforts properly.
A policy that has proven effective for New England states that Chesapeake Bay states could implement is Maine's Mandatory Shoreland Zoning Act. This act uses mechanisms to protect land near lakes, ponds and rivers from pollution and other environmental challenges. Creating a "Maryland Mandatory Shoreland Zoning Act" will enforce Chesapeake Bay farmlands in Maryland to administer shoreland zoning ordinances that regulate land use activity within 250 feet of horizontal distance from the water to eliminate any possible farm runoff.
Although making a shoreland zoning policy in Maryland could temporarily set back the productivity of farms within these newly zoned shorelines, nonmonetary sustainability costs, water quality and health safety outweigh any monetary costs and consequences. Protecting the future of local Chesapeake Bay community health, marine life and environment safety must be our priority over financial gain. Despite commendable voluntary efforts by organizations like the Chesapeake Bay Program, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and Environmental Engineers, the scale of the problem exceeds the current goals, highlighting the need for an enforceable policy.
Implementing a shoreland zoning policy may initially pose challenges and incur costs, but the long-term benefits to community health, marine life and environmental safety far outweigh the financial considerations. Chesapeake Bay watershed states like Maryland must consider enacting a Shoreland Zoning Act through the state legislature, with support and guidance from state environmental agencies. By prioritizing the protection of the Chesapeake Bay through proactive policy, we will ensure a safer and healthier future for all.
Elle Hogan is from Chevy Chase, Maryland, and grew up spending weekends and summers in Easton at her family's home on the Miles River. She is a first-year student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill where she plans to major in health policy and management.

title: Community celebrates Earth Day at Adkins Arboretum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Community celebrates Earth Day at Adkins Arboretum

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Swinging jazz, food, ecology and crafts for kids marked the outdoor Earth Day celebration on Saturday at Adkins Arboretum. There was also bird song from the woods and the sound of bullfrogs from the pond.The crowd was large, with 300 tickets sold for the event. Multiple environmental groups and government agencies hosted information tables.
Eastern Redbud saplings were given out for attendees to plant at home by Francis Smith of the Maryland Forest Service. There were master gardeners and monarch butterfly experts. A birding trip led into the forest in the morning.
"Earth Day heightens our awareness and appreciation. It is joyful and good to get out. And it is fun to host this site to share with other local nonprofits," said Ginna Tiernan, executive director of Adkins.
"It reminds us to breathe, step out in nature. It is incredible for your soul, your brain," Tiernan said. "It is amazing how clear you can think after a walk in the woods. I took a walk the other day, and a pileated woodpecker just swooped down in front of me. There were pine warblers in my ear. It is just affirming too that we are here on Earth with all of these animals, and we are a part of them."
Adkins celebrated the global holiday a little early this year, with Earth Day actually falling on Monday.
Earth Day is an annual event on April 22 to demonstrate support for environmental protection. First held on April 22, 1970, it now includes a wide range of events coordinated globally.
Jay Falstad, Adkins Arboretum board member and Executive Director of Queen Anne's Conservation Association, was using yellow and orange chalk to create a big sun at the arboretum's entrance.
"Earth Day is the one thing that we all share. We all share the same air, water and the same planet. We should all have an investment in protecting it," Falstad said.
There were many people who have worked hard to make this event happen. Not just organizing and planning but executing a fun educational experience.
Jenny Houghton, assistant director of Adkins Arboretum, said, "We are partnering with other environmental organizations. We thought it would be nice to show people that we are all working together. We have Pickering Creek, Tuckahoe State Park, Maryland DNR, Bartlett Tree Experts, Shore Rivers, Talbot County Master Gardeners and Phillips Wharf Environmental Center."
"The highlight is getting people outside to celebrate nature together and listening to great music, eating local food and hopefully scooping up some tadpoles in the wetland. It is good to remind ourselves that the Earth is worth taking care of, because it is all that we have got," said Houghton.
